studies.headline: Rudeness from the boss hurts differently than rudeness from a peer
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a two-week daily diary study with 132 full-time employees across a range of sectors, collecting 1,052 daily surveys that tracked small acts of incivility — being ignored, talked over, dismissed — alongside daily job satisfaction and three psychological needs: belonging, self-esteem and control. Incivility from supervisors had a broader daily impact than incivility from coworkers, eroding job satisfaction mainly by frustrating employees' sense of control and self-esteem. Coworker incivility produced a narrower threat profile, pointing more toward belonging.
studies.why_it_matters: Low-level rudeness is usually lumped together in engagement surveys and civility training, but this suggests the damage depends on who delivers it, and that the repair needed from a manager is different from the repair needed between peers.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers may want to audit their own micro-behaviors — the cut-off sentence, the unanswered message — separately from team-level civility norms, since the study suggests supervisor slights hit employees' sense of control and self-worth in a way peer slights do not. Daily-diary evidence shows associations within people over time, not a proven intervention, so treat it as a hypothesis to test locally.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone replaying a small workplace slight at night: the research suggests your reaction may be tracking something real about power. A dismissive comment from someone who controls your workload is psychologically a different event from the same comment from a colleague.
studies.caveats: Self-report only, with predictor and outcome from the same daily surveys (common-method bias); modest sample of 132 employees; two-week horizon; no causal test — day-level associations cannot rule out that low job satisfaction colors perceptions of incivility.
studies.paper_title: Workplace incivility's daily toll on job satisfaction: the mediating role of psychological need threats

studies.headline: Managers say work-related social media quietly rewrote the rules on being reachable
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted in-depth qualitative interviews with 67 managers about their use of work-oriented social networking platforms, analyzing the accounts through job demands-resources and boundary theory. They identified three distinct kinds of boundary blurring: professional versus personal identity, accessibility versus inaccessibility, and control versus autonomy. The same platforms that supplied useful resources — contacts, visibility, information — also generated demands that eroded the ability to be off duty.
studies.why_it_matters: Most organizational well-being policies address email and meetings, not the professional networking and messaging platforms where informal norms about availability are actually being set.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers could look at whether their organization's unwritten rules — who posts, who responds, how fast — are doing more to shape after-hours availability than any formal right-to-disconnect policy. The study points to a mismatch between stated well-being policies and informal cultural norms as the place to intervene.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The interviews describe a familiar bind: the networking that builds a career is the same activity that makes you permanently findable. It illustrates how the cost of professional visibility is increasingly paid in personal time and identity.
studies.caveats: Qualitative interview study — rich but not generalizable or quantifiable; managers only, so the experience of non-managerial staff is missing; retrospective self-report; no measurement of actual well-being outcomes.
studies.paper_title: Job Demands‐Resources, Well‐Being and Work‐Life Boundaries: The Pervasiveness of Social Networking Platforms

studies.headline: Repetitive tasks may be the hidden hub that keeps job worries running after hours
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 573 employed young adults in China twice over 60 days, measuring job demands, job insecurity, perceived employability and work-related rumination, then mapped how these elements predicted each other over time using cross-lagged panel network analysis. Task repetitiveness emerged as the strongest bridging node — the variable that most connected different parts of the psychological system. Job demands, job insecurity and affective (emotional, brooding) rumination formed the dense core, while perceived employability and problem-solving rumination sat on the periphery, relatively disconnected.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that interventions aimed at helping employees 'switch off' may be targeting the wrong node: monotonous, repetitive work appears to be a transmission point feeding insecurity and after-hours brooding.
studies.story_angle_primary: Instead of yet another detachment workshop, managers could test whether rotating or varying repetitive tasks reduces the after-hours rumination their teams report. The analysis also suggests that boosting employees' confidence in their external employability may not do much to interrupt the brooding cycle — it sat at the edge of the network.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you can't stop thinking about work in the evening, the content of your job — how repetitive it is — may matter more than your workload or your willpower. The study also distinguishes productive problem-solving thought from emotional brooding, and only the latter was tangled up with insecurity.
studies.caveats: Self-report only across both waves (common-method bias); two measurement points over 60 days is a short horizon for causal inference; single country (China) and a single age group (young employees); network analysis identifies structural position, not proven causal mechanisms.
studies.paper_title: Under pressure, thoughts remain unsettled: why uncertain work environments prevent employees from psychologically detaching after work

fact_check.headline: Rudeness from the boss hurts differently than rudeness from a peer
fact_check.notes: Design, sample (132 employees, 1,052 daily surveys) and the headline supervisor finding match the abstract. Two small over-readings: the specific claim that coworker incivility points toward belonging, and the implied null for peers on control/self-esteem, are not stated in the abstract. Caveats appropriately flag common-method bias and the absence of causal evidence.

issues.label: Coworker threat profile specified beyond abstract
issues.as_written: Coworker incivility produced a narrower threat profile, pointing more toward belonging.
issues.abstract_says: Results show that the source of incivility shapes the nature and severity of psychological need threats. Supervisor incivility has a broader impact than coworker incivility, primarily reducing job satisfaction through control and self-esteem frustration. ... identifying distinct threat profiles for supervisor versus coworker incivility.
issues.problem: The abstract confirms distinct profiles and a narrower impact for coworker incivility but never names belonging as the need coworker incivility threatens. Unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Say coworker incivility produced a narrower threat profile, without naming which need, or attribute the belonging detail to the full paper.

issues.label: Implied null effect for peer incivility
issues.as_written: supervisor slights hit employees' sense of control and self-worth in a way peer slights do not
issues.abstract_says: Supervisor incivility has a broader impact than coworker incivility, primarily reducing job satisfaction through control and self-esteem frustration.
issues.problem: The abstract reports a broader impact for supervisor incivility, not an absence of control/self-esteem effects for coworker incivility; the digest asserts a null the abstract does not report.
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to 'hit employees' sense of control and self-worth more broadly than peer slights do.'

fact_check.headline: Managers say work-related social media quietly rewrote the rules on being reachable
fact_check.notes: Method (qualitative interviews, 67 managers), theoretical framing (JD-R plus boundary theory) and the three boundary-blurring dimensions are reported accurately, as is the policy/informal-norms implication. Only the itemized list of resources goes beyond the abstract.

issues.label: Specific resources not named in abstract
issues.as_written: The same platforms that supplied useful resources — contacts, visibility, information — also generated demands that eroded the ability to be off duty.
issues.abstract_says: we highlight the impact of work-oriented SN on job demands, resources, work-life boundaries, and well-being
issues.problem: The abstract refers to resources and demands generically; the specific resources (contacts, visibility, information) are the digest's elaboration. Unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Drop the itemized examples or mark them as illustrative rather than findings.

fact_check.headline: Repetitive tasks may be the hidden hub that keeps job worries running after hours
fact_check.notes: Sample (573 employed young adults in China), 60-day two-wave design and cross-lagged panel network analysis match, as do the bridging role of task repetitiveness and the central/peripheral structure. The list of measured variables omits job stress/task repetitiveness, and one reader-facing line turns bridging capacity into a claim that repetitiveness outweighs workload.

issues.label: Measured variables listed imprecisely
issues.as_written: measuring job demands, job insecurity, perceived employability and work-related rumination
issues.abstract_says: examine the longitudinal relationships among job stress, job insecurity, perceived employability, and work-related rumination ... task repetitiveness shows the strongest bridging capacity
issues.problem: The abstract frames the constructs as job stress (with task repetitiveness and job demands as components in the network); the digest's list omits task repetitiveness, the variable the story is built on, and substitutes 'job demands' for 'job stress'.
issues.suggested_fix: List the constructs as job stress (including task repetitiveness and job demands), job insecurity, perceived employability and work-related rumination.

issues.label: Bridging position treated as relative importance
issues.as_written: the content of your job — how repetitive it is — may matter more than your workload or your willpower
issues.abstract_says: task repetitiveness shows the strongest bridging capacity and information diffusion function ... Job demands, job insecurity, and affective rumination jointly form the central structure of the system
issues.problem: Strongest bridging capacity means repetitiveness connects subsystems, not that it matters more than workload; job demands are themselves part of the central structure.
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to 'how repetitive your job is may be more tightly linked to after-hours brooding than you would expect', avoiding a ranking against workload.

sections.trends:
**Convergent findings**
- *Digital micro-boundaries are where recovery is actually won or lost.* "Managers say work-related social media quietly rewrote the rules on being reachable" (W7224150475) sits directly alongside the previous digest's "Answering email on the morning commute helps; doing it on the way home doesn't" (W7223307249). Both locate the action in small, repeated, technology-mediated transitions rather than in formal policy or trait recovery capacity — and both find the same behavior can be resource and demand at once, depending on direction or context.
- *The manager is a source of strain as well as a carrier of it.* "Rudeness from the boss hurts differently than rudeness from a peer" (W7225859305) is the mirror image of "Faking the supportive-boss face costs managers; genuinely feeling it doesn't" (W7223665250). Last run priced the cost to the manager of performing support; this run shows what the manager's unperformed micro-behavior costs the employee, and specifies the channel — control and self-esteem rather than belonging.

**Advances**
- *From "when work follows you home" to "what in the work follows you home."* "Repetitive tasks may be the hidden hub that keeps job worries running after hours" (W7224080358) advances the boundary thread beyond W7223307249's timing-of-transition framing by pointing at job content: task repetitiveness as the strongest bridging node feeding insecurity and affective rumination. It also sharpens the outcome, separating brooding from problem-solving thought — a distinction the commute study did not make.
- *Source and channel specificity.* W7225859305 does for incivility what W7223665250 did for emotional labor last run: break an undifferentiated construct into components with different consequences (supervisor versus coworker; control/self-esteem versus belonging).

**Counterpoints**
- *Employability confidence may be the wrong lever.* W7224080358 places perceived employability on the periphery of the network, relatively disconnected from the insecurity–rumination core. That is a quiet brake on the career-agency optimism running through the previous digest's autonomy and onboarding findings (W7212031246, W7223449472) — feeling marketable did not look like it interrupts the brooding cycle.

**New themes**
- *Work-oriented social networking platforms as an unregulated well-being frontier* (W7224150475). The previous digest covered email, messaging and commute device use; nothing in it addressed professional networking platforms, where availability norms are informal rather than policy-set.
- *Network methods and "which node to target."* W7224080358 introduces cross-lagged panel network analysis — a shift from asking whether a variable matters to asking where in the system to intervene. Nothing in the previous digest used this approach.
sections.feature_pitch:
**The pattern:** All three studies suggest that the things keeping work lodged in people's heads are not the ones well-being policy targets. Supervisor micro-slights do more damage than peer slights and do it through control and self-worth (W7225859305); informal norms on professional networking platforms are setting availability expectations that formal policies never touch (W7224150475); and task repetitiveness, not workload, emerges as the hub node feeding job insecurity and after-hours brooding, with employability confidence sitting uselessly on the periphery (W7224080358). Taken together: the off switch is relational, informal and built into job content — not in the inbox.

**Why pitch this now:** Right-to-disconnect rules are live or advancing in Australia, Ontario and across the EU, and almost all of them are written around email and after-hours contact; meanwhile AI deployment is flattening a lot of jobs into higher-volume repetitive execution, which is precisely the variable this batch flags as the transmission point.

**Angle:** A reported feature on why "switch off" policies keep underperforming — that disconnection is governed by who your boss is, what the unwritten platform norms are, and how monotonous the work itself is, none of which a policy document reaches. Primary fit is business and management readers responsible for well-being programs; a general-interest version works for anyone who has followed every piece of switching-off advice and still lies awake.

**Potential headlines:**
- The research says three things keep work in your head after hours, and email isn't one of them
- Right-to-disconnect laws are aimed at the wrong part of the job
- Why you still can't stop thinking about work, even with the notifications off

**Potential outlets:**
- *MIT Sloan Management Review* — the "which node do you actually intervene on" framing, drawn from the network analysis, suits its appetite for rethinking how organizations choose well-being interventions.
- *Business Insider* — strong on right-to-disconnect and always-on culture; this is the evidence-based complication of a story it already runs, with the professional-networking-platform finding as the fresh hook.
- *Wired* — the work-oriented social networking material fits its coverage of how platform norms, not policies, end up governing behavior.
- *The Guardian* (work and careers) — has covered disconnection legislation closely and would run a general-interest piece arguing the laws miss the mechanism, with the repetitive-work finding giving it a job-quality edge.
sections.pitch_ideas:
- **Rudeness from the boss hurts differently than rudeness from a peer (Work ID W7225859305):** Lead with the asymmetry — a dismissive comment from someone who controls your workload hits control and self-esteem, while the same comment from a colleague mostly threatens belonging, which means civility training that treats both the same is mistargeted; for a manager-audience leadership column, or a work-psychology explainer in a general-interest or women's/lifestyle outlet on why small slights from a boss linger, with the self-report and two-week limits stated.
- **Managers say work-related social media quietly rewrote the rules on being reachable (Work ID W7224150475):** The angle is the gap between formal disconnection policy and informal platform norms — 67 managers describe professional visibility being paid for in personal time and identity; for an HR explainer on well-being policy blind spots, or a career-advice column on the cost of being permanently findable.
- **Repetitive tasks may be the hidden hub that keeps job worries running after hours (Work ID W7224080358):** The counterintuitive lever — if your team can't stop ruminating, vary the work before you book another detachment workshop, and note that boosting employability confidence sat at the edge of the network; for a manager-audience column on job design, or a career-advice piece distinguishing productive problem-solving thought from brooding, flagged as a two-wave study of young employees in a single country.
